newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish prime minister to visit Israel.
newsitem.headline: Polish prime minister to visit Israel.

text.p: Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz visits Israel this week, pressing on with Warsaw's efforts to build on past centuries of shared Polish-Jewish history to promote closer economic and other ties now.

After talks with Israeli political and business leaders from Tuesday to Thursday, Cimoszewicz will meet Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat on Friday, to discuss current prospects for building Palestinian self-rule.

"This is a visit of...great interest for both sides. For historical reasons, Poland is a partner for Israel," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Pawel Dobrowolski, referring to the centuries when Poland was home to millions of Jews before World War Two Nazi German invaders inflicted the Holocaust.

The current ex-communist government and President Aleksander Kwasniewski have laid special stress on Poland's post-1989 policy of building understanding with the Jewish diaspora and with Israel, where many citizens stem from Poland.
Cimoszewicz is to hold talks with his counterpart Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem on Tuesday, and will also meet parliamentarians, President Ezer Weizman and business groups.

Dobrowolski said Poland, a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, had an interest in the Middle East peace process, not least because it had peace-keeping troops there whom Cimoszewicz would visit on the Golan Heights.
Bilateral issues to be discussed during the trip include promoting Israeli investment and economic links, further freeing up trade, and correcting a mounting trade imbalance.

The Foreign Ministry says Polish exports to Israel in 1995 were worth $20.7 million and imports $65 million, while in the first nine months of last year the figures were $12.1 million of exports and $61.3 million of imports from Israel.

Poland plans to buy the NT-D anti-tank missile, now being developed by Israel's Rafael, for its new Huzar attack helicopter, but some critics say the government should opt for a fully-tested alternative rather than clinch this deal.
Polish Defence Minister Stanislaw Dobrzanski is travelling with Cimoszewicz and is likely to discuss the fate of this major deal as well as other defence industry cooperation.
Poland wants visa-free travel with Israel, but this has been delayed because Israel says up to 20,000 Poles are working illegally there and wants to resolve this issue first.
A key theme of the visit will be Poland's efforts to clear up issues clouding relations with Jewish communities abroad.

Cimoszewicz and other Polish leaders apologised last year for a 1946 pogrom which prompted many Jews to emigrate and for anti-Semitic episodes in Poland's past -- while calling for an end to a stereotype of all Poles as anti-Semitic.
The government last year also adopted a plan to better conserve the former Auschwitz-Birkenau Nazi German death camp.
A continued subject of debate is the return of former Jewish property which was taken over by Poland's communist authorities after World War Two.

A bill now before parliament will restore some communal religious properties such as synagogues to the few, tiny remaining Jewish congregations, but Jewish organisations abroad would like some of this to reach Polish Jews living abroad.

Poland also insists that when passes laws to return private property or compensates former owners, Jews will be treated like other Poles and only resident citizens will be eligible. Foreign Jewish organisations say this is unfair.
Cimoszewicz is scheduled to meet the World Jewish Restitution Organisation on Tuesday to discuss these questions.
